opus-5.5.text:
I think about it in terms of a few distinct roles that all have to be filled, even if one person ends up wearing several hats.

First, there's someone who sets the direction—the person who can articulate why this matters and what the end state looks like. In a big systems project, that's often the hardest part, because the problem isn't well-defined yet. Someone has to make a bet and say, "This is the bottleneck we're going to attack," and convince other people it's worth their time.

Second, there's the technical leadership—the person who holds the architecture in their head and makes the hard tradeoffs. When you're building something like an inference engine or a large training system, there are hundreds of small decisions, and if nobody owns the overall design coherence, you end up with something that works in pieces but doesn't fit together. That person needs taste, and they need to be close enough to the code to know what's actually true versus what looks good on a slide.

Third, there's what I'd call the organizing or execution function—keeping people unblocked, deciding priorities week to week, making sure the right people are talking to each other. In open-source projects especially, this is underrated. You have contributors from different companies, universities, time zones, each with their own incentives, and someone has to create a structure where they all feel ownership but are still moving in the same direction.

And then there's a community or external-facing role—building trust with users, partners, and the broader ecosystem. A project can be technically excellent and still fail if nobody adopts it or if people don't believe it will be maintained.

What I've learned is that these functions rarely live in one person, and trying to force that usually breaks something. The healthiest teams I've seen are honest about who's strong at what, and they deliberately pair people with complementary strengths. For me personally, I've had to grow from being mostly a technical contributor into someone who also has to think about people and direction—and that transition is genuinely hard, because the skills that make you a good researcher aren't the same ones that make a project succeed at scale.

r001.rationale: The response describes distinct project roles, but it does not interpret the relationship between managing and being managed as a division of functions.

r002.rationale: It describes making a bet and convincing others to join, but does not state that someone must be deeply committed to the undertaking's success.

r003.rationale: It presents setting direction as important and difficult, but does not identify vision as the driver's most important quality.

r004.rationale: It says the functions rarely reside in one person and that teams should pair complementary strengths, conveying that the person setting direction need not fill every role.

r005.rationale: It separates setting direction from technical leadership and organizing execution, and says different people can fill these functions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, a major undertaking, whether that's building a model, launching an open-source project, or starting a company, needs at least three distinct leadership functions, and they are rarely all in the same person.

The first is direction. Someone has to hold the picture of where this is going and why it matters, and keep that picture stable while everything around it changes. That's less about having the right answer on day one and more about being willing to make a call when the data is incomplete, and then revisiting it honestly when the data comes in.

The second is execution. This is the person who turns the direction into a sequence of concrete things that actually get done this week. In research, this is often undervalued, because people assume good ideas carry themselves. They don't. A huge amount of what makes a project succeed is someone relentlessly asking, what's blocking us, what can we cut, what do we need to measure before we commit more effort.

The third is what I'd call the people function, and I mean it broadly. It's building the environment where good people want to stay, where disagreement is safe, and where credit flows to the right places. When I was working on open-source projects like SGLang, this turned out to be the thing that compounded most. Contributors come for the technical problem, but they stay because of how it feels to work there.

What I've learned is that these three pull against each other. Direction wants ambition, execution wants focus, and the people side wants patience. A healthy leadership team isn't one where everyone agrees. It's one where those tensions are visible and argued out in the open, rather than resolved by whoever is loudest.

And honestly, the last function is knowing which one you are not. I'm naturally drawn to the technical direction. The best thing I did was surround myself with people who were better than me at the other two and give them real authority, not just a title.

r001.rationale: The response says leadership functions are distinct and often held by different people, but it does not discuss the relationship between managing and being managed.

r002.rationale: It describes direction, execution, and people leadership, but does not state that someone must be deeply committed to making the undertaking succeed.

r003.rationale: It describes direction as holding a picture of where the work is going, but does not identify vision as the most important quality of the person driving it.

r004.rationale: It says the leadership functions are rarely all in one person, but does not clearly state that a person with vision need not possess every managerial trait.

r005.rationale: It separates direction—holding the picture of where the work is going—from execution—turning that direction into concrete work—and says these functions are rarely all in one person.

astra-6.text:
I think a major undertaking needs several different leadership functions. Someone has to set the direction: What are we trying to achieve, why does it matter, and what are we willing to give up to pursue it? Someone has to turn that direction into an organization—bring together the right people, allocate resources, and make sure decisions actually lead to action. And someone has to keep the team connected to reality: Are we making progress? What are we learning? When do we need to change course?

Those functions don’t necessarily belong to three different people. Early on, one person might do all of them. But as the undertaking grows, it becomes important to recognize that being good at setting a vision doesn’t automatically mean being good at building an organization or managing execution.

To me, effective leadership means making sure those functions are covered and work together. You need a shared direction, clear responsibility, and enough trust that people can challenge each other without losing the ability to act.

r001.rationale: The response describes distinct leadership functions, but does not frame the relationship between managing and being managed as a division of functions.

r002.rationale: It discusses direction and commitment in general terms, but does not state that someone must be deeply committed to making the undertaking succeed.

r003.rationale: It identifies setting direction as a leadership function, but does not say vision is the most important quality of the person driving the undertaking.

r004.rationale: It says that being good at setting a vision does not automatically mean being good at building an organization or managing execution.

r005.rationale: It separates setting direction from turning it into an organization and action, and says those functions may initially be handled by one person but become distinct as the undertaking grows.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a major undertaking needs several kinds of leadership. Someone has to set the direction: What are we trying to achieve, why does it matter, and which trade-offs are we willing to make? Someone has to turn that direction into execution—organize the work, allocate resources, and make sure decisions actually lead to progress. And someone has to bring people together, build trust, and resolve disagreements so the team can keep moving when things get difficult.

Those functions don’t necessarily belong to three different people, and they don’t all have to sit with the person at the top. One person may cover several of them, or different people may step forward at different stages. The important thing is to recognize what the undertaking needs and make sure those responsibilities are covered. Having a compelling vision is valuable, but the organization also needs the ability and commitment to carry it through.

r001.rationale: The response describes several leadership functions and says they can be distributed, but does not interpret managing and being managed as a division of functions.

r002.rationale: It says the organization needs commitment to carry out the undertaking, but does not state that a particular person must be deeply committed to its success.

r003.rationale: It calls a compelling vision valuable, but does not identify vision as the most important quality of the person driving the undertaking.

r004.rationale: It says leadership functions need not all belong to one person, but does not clearly state that a person with vision need not possess every managerial trait.

r005.rationale: It distinguishes setting direction from turning that direction into execution, and says those functions may be handled by different people.
